title: Things fall: everything drops when we let go

summary.text: Let go of a spoon, and it falls. Let go of a feather or a balloon, and it falls too, only slowly. Your child drops ten everyday things and finds that every one of them falls down. The Earth pulls everything towards it, and scientists call this pull gravity. A thing stays up only while something holds it: a hand, a shelf, a string or the floor.
summary.art: A girl standing in a kitchen with her hand open, and a steel spoon, a feather, a jasmine flower and a balloon all falling towards a steel plate on the floor.

intro.hook: Hold a spoon up high. Open your hand. What happens? Now try it with a feather or a balloon. Does that fall too?
intro.text: Try the spoon first. Then try a feather and a balloon. Do they all fall? In this unit you let go of many things and watch where they go. You find out what holds things up. And you learn the name scientists give to the pull that makes things fall.
intro.art: A child's open hand high above a steel plate, with a steel spoon just leaving the fingers.

outcomes: By the end I can show that everything falls when I let go of it, some things fast and some slowly.
By the end I can say that the Earth pulls everything down, and that scientists call this pull gravity.
By the end I can find what is holding a thing up, and say what happens when that holder is taken away.
By the end I can show that a dropped thing falls straight down, to the spot under my hand.
By the end I can spot falling things around me: rain, leaves, water from a tap and my own jumps.

terms.meaning: To fall is to move down towards the ground when nothing holds you up.
terms.example: A mango falls from the tree. A spoon falls off the table.
terms.art: A ripe yellow mango falling from a branch towards the grass.

terms.meaning: Gravity is the pull of the Earth. It pulls everything towards the ground.
terms.example: Gravity makes the rain fall and brings you down after a jump.
terms.art: A girl in the middle of a jump, with a big friendly arrow pointing down to the ground under her feet.

terms.meaning: A support is something that holds a thing up and stops it falling.
terms.example: The shelf is a support for the books. The floor is a support for you.
terms.art: A wooden shelf holding up a row of books and a steel tumbler.

explanations.concept: Everything falls when we let go
explanations.definition: When nothing holds a thing up, it falls down. The Earth pulls everything towards it. Scientists call this pull gravity.
explanations.description: In the Let-Go Test you let go of ten things. The spoon fell. The rice fell. The water fell. Even the feather and the balloon fell, only slowly. Nothing stayed up. The Earth pulls everything down, and nobody has to touch the spoon for it to pull.
examples: In the Let-Go Test, the spoon, the bottle cap and the lemon fell fast.
In the Let-Go Test, the feather and the balloon fell slowly, but they still landed.
Rain falls from the clouds. Mangoes and coconuts fall from trees.
explanations.context: This card is about the Let-Go Test, where you let go of ten things, one at a time.
explanations.art: A row of things falling side by side: a spoon, a lemon, a bottle cap, grains of rice and a feather, with the feather a little higher than the rest.

explanations.concept: A thing stays up only while something holds it
explanations.definition: A thing that is not falling is being held up. A hand, a shelf, a string, a hook or the floor holds it. Something that holds a thing up is called a support.
explanations.description: In Take Away the Holder, a tumbler sat on a book. It did not fall, because the book held it up. When the book was pulled away, the tumbler fell. The Earth pulls the fan, the clock and you too. Each one stays up because a support holds it.
examples: In Take Away the Holder, the tumbler stayed up on the book, and fell when the book went.
Clothes on a washing line are held up by the pegs and the line.
When you sit on a chair, the chair is your support.
explanations.context: This card is about Take Away the Holder, where a tumbler sat on a book until the book was pulled away.
explanations.art: A grown-up's hands sliding a book sideways from under a steel tumbler, and the tumbler starting to fall towards a cushion.

explanations.definition: A dropped thing falls straight down, to the spot right under where you let go. Down means towards the ground, the Earth.
explanations.description: In Right on the Dot, you held a lemon above a dot and let go. It landed on the dot, or very close. It fell straight down. A sheet of paper rocked and slid sideways, because the air pushed it about. It still came down.
examples: In Right on the Dot, the lemon landed on the dot under your hand.
Water from a tap falls straight down into the bucket.
A sheet of paper rocks from side to side, but it still lands on the floor.
explanations.context: This card is about Right on the Dot, where you dropped a lemon onto a dot on a newspaper.
explanations.art: A lemon falling in a straight line from a child's fingers onto a big chalk dot on a sheet of newspaper.

explanations.concept: Some things fall slowly, but they still fall
explanations.definition: Feathers, paper, cotton and blown-up balloons fall slowly, because the air gets in their way. They still fall to the ground.
explanations.description: Air is all around us. You cannot see it, but it is there. A light, wide thing like a feather has to push through the air as it falls, so the air slows it down. A balloon from a fair is filled with helium gas, which is lighter than air. The air around pushes that balloon up. When the helium leaks out, it comes down.
examples: In the Let-Go Test, the feather rocked slowly down and landed.
A blown-up balloon floats down and bumps gently on the floor.
A helium balloon from a fair goes up, because the heavier air pushes it up.
explanations.context: This card is about the slow fallers in the Let-Go Test: the feather, the cotton and the balloon.
explanations.art: A feather and a blown-up balloon drifting slowly down beside a steel spoon that has already landed on a plate.

explanations.description: We know what gravity does. It makes things fall, and it keeps the Moon going round the Earth. But how does the Earth pull a spoon without touching it? Scientists have two big ideas, and both give the same answers for spoons and mangoes. No one yet knows what gravity is at the very smallest size.
examples: Gravity pulls the spoon down, without touching it.
Gravity pulls the Moon too, and keeps the Moon going round the Earth.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in 1687
perspectives.explanation: Everything pulls on everything else. The Earth is very big, so its pull is strong, and things fall towards it.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein, a scientist born in Germany, in 1915
perspectives.explanation: The Earth bends space and time around it, a little like a heavy ball sitting on a bedsheet. Things near the Earth roll into that bend, and we see them fall.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists are still working on: what gravity really is.
explanations.art: The Earth with a spoon falling towards it, and a bedsheet behind with a heavy ball making a dip in the middle.

agreed.text: Everything near the Earth is pulled towards it. This pull is called gravity.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it. Spoons, rice, water, feathers and balloons all fall when let go. Falling needs no air: astronauts on the Moon, where there is no air, dropped things, and the Moon's pull brought them down.

agreed.text: A thing that is not falling is held up by a support.
agreed.evidence: Take the support away, and the thing falls at once. Builders and engineers plan every building so that its floors, walls and pillars hold up everything above them.

agreed.text: Air slows down light, wide things as they fall.
agreed.evidence: A flat sheet of paper drifts down slowly, but the same sheet squashed into a tight ball falls much faster. The paper weighs the same, so the difference comes from the air.

challenging.claim: Light things like feathers and balloons do not fall. They float.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children, and many grown-ups too
challenging.for: A feather drifts in the air for a long time. A balloon seems to hang there.
challenging.against: Watch to the end. In the Let-Go Test the feather and the balloon both landed on the floor. They fall slowly because the air gets in their way, but they do fall.
challenging.context: This card is about feathers and balloons, which seem to float.

challenging.claim: Things fall because the air pushes them down.
challenging.for: Air is all around us, and we cannot see what is pulling the spoon.
challenging.against: The air does the opposite: it slows falling things down. On the Moon there is no air, and dropped things still fall. It is the pull of the ground below, gravity, that makes things fall.
challenging.context: This card is about what makes a spoon fall.

challenging.claim: Smoke, air and fire go up by nature. The Earth does not pull them down.
challenging.who: The Greek thinker Aristotle, about 2,350 years ago, and many people after him
challenging.for: Smoke from an agarbatti rises up to the ceiling. A flame always points up.
challenging.against: In 1638, Galileo wrote that air has weight, so the Earth pulls air too. Hot, smoky air rises only because the cooler, heavier air around it sinks under it and pushes it up.
challenging.context: This card is about smoke and flames, which go up instead of down.

big_questions.q: A tumbler sits still on the table. Is the Earth pulling on it right now? How could you find out?
big_questions.hint: Think about Take Away the Holder. What happened the moment the book went?

big_questions.q: Why does a feather fall slowly, when a spoon falls fast?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air the feather has to push through. Squash a sheet of paper into a ball and drop it. Does it fall faster now?

big_questions.q: If you dug a hole right through the Earth and dropped a ball in, which way would it fall?
big_questions.hint: Down always means towards the Earth. What is 'down' for a child on the other side of the world?

big_questions.q: Is there anywhere you could go where nothing would fall?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Moon, where astronauts dropped things. Think about deep space, very far from every star and planet.

story.title: Nila and the Falling Spoon
story.note: Nila, Arul and Paati are made up. Paati means grandmother in Tamil, and malli is jasmine. Kites, big brown birds of prey, really do circle over Chennai and many Indian cities.
text: Nila was six. She lived in a flat on the fourth floor of a building in Chennai. From her window she could see coconut trees, a big water tank and a lot of sky.
Her baby brother Arul was one year old. Every morning he sat in his high chair and ate soft idli. And every morning he did the same thing.
He held his spoon up high. He opened his hand. Clang! The spoon fell onto the floor.
'Why does he keep doing that?' asked Nila.
Paati was drinking her coffee. 'He is doing a test,' she said. 'Babies drop things again and again. They are finding out what happens.'
'But the spoon always falls,' said Nila. 'Every single time.'
'Does everything fall?' asked Paati. 'Or only spoons?'
Nila wanted to know. She found a small feather poking out of an old cushion. She held it up high and let go. The feather rocked from side to side, slowly, slowly. Then it lay on the floor.
She took one jasmine flower from Paati's string of malli. She let go. The flower fell, soft and quick, and landed by Arul's chair.

Then she found her birthday balloon behind the sofa. 'Balloons float,' she told Arul. She held it up and let go. The balloon drifted down, slowly, and bumped onto the floor. Arul laughed and kicked his feet.
'Even the balloon fell!' said Nila.

She went to the window. High above the water tank, a big brown bird was going round and round. She was a kite, a kind of bird, not the paper kind. Her wings were spread out wide. She was not falling at all.
'Paati! That bird is not falling!'
Paati came to the window. 'Watch her wings,' she said. 'Her wings push the air down, and the air pushes her up. The air is holding her, the way your hand holds a spoon.'
Just then the kite tucked her wings in a little. Down she swooped, towards the coconut trees. Then she spread them wide again and sailed up.
Nila thought about this all day. At lunch, she looked at her plate. The table was holding it up. The ceiling was holding up the fan. A nail was holding up the clock.
At dinner, Arul held his spoon up high again. This time Nila was ready. She put her hand under his. He opened his fingers, and the spoon fell, right into her palm.
'You see, Arul,' said Nila. 'Everything falls. The feather, the flower and even the balloon. The spoon falls too, unless someone holds it. Tonight I am the one holding it.'
Paati smiled. 'Scientists have a name for the Earth's pull,' she said. 'They call it gravity.'
That night, Nila lay in bed. The bed held her up. The floor held the bed. The building held the floor, and the ground held the building. And under them all, the Earth was pulling, all the time.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Nila finds that everything she lets go of falls, even a feather and a balloon. Things that stay up are always held by something: a hand, a table, a nail, the floor, or the air under a bird's wings. The pull is there all the time, and we only see it when the holder goes.
ask: What did Arul keep doing with his spoon? Why did Paati say he was doing a test?
Which things did Nila drop? Did any of them stay up?
Why was the kite bird not falling?
At dinner, what held up Arul's spoon?
art: A baby boy in a high chair at a breakfast table with idli, holding a steel spoon high, and his sister watching.
A girl letting go of a feather, a jasmine flower and a balloon in a sunny flat, all drifting down.
A grandmother and a girl at a window, looking at a big brown kite bird circling over coconut trees and a water tank.
The girl's hand under her baby brother's hand, catching a falling spoon, both of them laughing.

games.title: Fast, Slow or Up? The let-go card game
games.players: 2 or more players. Take turns being the reader.
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows something being let go of. Players guess what it will do: fall fast, fall slowly, or go up.

items.f: Let go of a steel spoon
items.b: FAST. It falls straight down, clang.
SLOW. It rocks from side to side, then lands.

items.f: A ripe mango comes off the tree
items.b: FAST. It falls straight down to the ground.

items.f: Let go of a ball of cotton wool
items.b: SLOW. The air slows it, but it lands.
FAST. Rain falls all the way down to the ground.

items.f: Let go of a balloon you blew up
items.b: SLOW. It drifts down and bumps on the floor.

items.f: Let go of a flat sheet of paper
items.b: SLOW. It swings about, then lands.

items.f: Let go of a soap bubble
items.b: SLOW. It sinks slowly, or pops on the way.
UP. The hot smoky air is lighter than the air around it, and the heavier air pushes it up.

items.f: Let go of a helium balloon from a fair
items.b: UP. The heavier air around it pushes it up. When the helium leaks out, it comes down.

items.f: A kite bird folds her wings
items.b: FAST. Without her wings spread on the air, she swoops down.

printables.title: 12 answer tokens: 3 for each of up to 4 players

rules: Cut out the 12 cards. Mix them and put them in a pile, question side up.
Cut out the tokens. Each player takes one set of three: FAST, SLOW and UP.
Take turns to be the reader. The reader reads the top card out loud. A grown-up reads for a child who cannot read yet.
Every player, the reader too, holds up one token at the same time. The reader keeps the back of the card hidden.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. Everyone with the right token gets a point. Say why for a bonus point.
If you are not sure, try it with a real spoon, paper or ball afterwards.
Pass the pile to the next reader after each card. Play until all 12 cards are read. The player with the most points wins. If points are equal, everyone wins.

setup.art: A girl holding up a card that says Let go of a feather, and two children holding up wavy SLOW tokens.
setup.caption: 1. Read a card. Everyone holds up a token.

setup.art: The girl turning the card over to show SLOW, and a boy cheering.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the card. Who was right?

flow.do: Read the rules. Show the three tokens.
flow.say: Here are three tokens. FAST means it falls quickly. SLOW means it falls slowly. UP means it goes up. Ready?
flow.kid: FAST, SLOW or UP. Hold up the one you think.

flow.do: Play all 12 cards. After each card, ask one player why. Swap the reader each time.
flow.say: Let go of a balloon you blew up. Fast, slow or up? Show me. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Hold up a token. Say why.

ask.q: Why does the balloon you blew up fall slowly?

flow.parent: The helium balloon and the agarbatti smoke are the tricky cards. Both go up only because the heavier air around them pushes them up. Nothing is pulling them up.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last question, and it is a hard one.
flow.kid: Answer the last one.

check.q: A girl called Meenakshi throws a ball up into the air. What happens to it?
options: It goes up, then falls back down
It goes up and stays up
check.why: Her throw pushes the ball up. The Earth keeps pulling it, so it slows down, stops for a moment and falls back.

games.title: Catch It Before It Lands
games.players: 1 or more children and one dropper.
games.context: This is a catching game. A grown-up drops things from up high, and you try to catch each one before it touches the floor.

printables.title: Catch score sheet
items: Thing dropped | Try 1 | Try 2 | Try 3 | How many caught?
A sock rolled into a ball | | | |

rules: The dropper stands on the floor and holds one thing up as high as they can reach.
The catcher stands one big step away, with their hands down by their sides.
The dropper says 'Ready, go!' and opens their hand.
The catcher tries to catch the thing before it touches the floor. A catch scores one tick.
Each thing gets three tries. Then swap to the next thing.
At the end, count the ticks. Which thing was easiest to catch? Which was hardest?

setup.art: A mother holding a hanky high above her head, and her daughter one step away, hands at her sides, ready.
setup.caption: 1. The dropper holds it up high.

setup.art: The daughter diving to catch a rolled-up sock just above the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Catch it before it lands!

flow.do: Read the rules. Stand one big step apart.
flow.say: I will hold things up high and let go. You catch them before they touch the floor. Hands down by your sides to start.
flow.kid: Hands down. When I let go, catch it before it lands!

flow.do: Drop each thing three times: the hanky, the balloon, the sock ball, the soft toy. Tick each catch on the score sheet.
flow.say: Ready, go! Did you catch it? Which one is easier, the hanky or the sock ball? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Ready? Catch it! Was that one easy or hard?

ask.q: Why was the hanky easier to catch?
good: The air slows it down, so I have more time.

flow.parent: Drop, never throw, so it is fair. Slow fallers like the hanky and the balloon are easy to catch. The sock ball falls fast, so it is hard.

flow.do: Count the ticks together. Then the check question.
flow.say: Which thing did you catch most? Did any of them stay up in the air and wait for you?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Did anything stay up and wait?

check.q: A girl called Jyoti is catching a hanky and a sock ball. Which one gives her more time to catch it?
check.why: The hanky falls slowly, because the air slows it. The sock ball falls fast. Both fall, but the hanky takes longer.

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. Does it fall fast or slowly when you let go? Colour the fast ones red and the slow ones blue.
items.why: Small, solid things fall fast. Light, wide things are slowed by the air, so they fall slowly. A strong answer knows that all six fall.

items.p: Draw one thing you let go of in the Let-Go Test. Draw an arrow to show which way it went.
items.a: Any thing from the test, with an arrow pointing down.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the thing and an arrow pointing down, towards the floor.

items.p: A feather never falls. It floats in the air for ever.
items.why: False. In the Let-Go Test, the feather drifted slowly, but it landed in the end. The air slows a feather, but the Earth still pulls it down.

items.p: When you jump, the Earth stops pulling you for a moment.
items.why: False. The Earth pulls you all the time. You go up because your legs push, and the Earth's pull brings you back down.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to the support that holds it up.
items.why: Each thing stays up only because its support holds it. A strong answer can say what would happen if the support were taken away.
items.art: A ceiling fan, a wall clock, clothes on a line and a sitting child on the left, and a hook, a nail, pegs and a chair on the right.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the tumbler fall when the book was pulled away?
items.a: The book was holding it up. When the book went, nothing held it, so the Earth pulled it down.
items.why: A strong answer says the book held the tumbler up, and that the Earth's pull made it fall once nothing held it.

items.p: A girl called Mohini lets go of a mango and a feather from the same height at the same time. Which one reaches the floor first?
items.why: The mango lands first. The air slows the feather, so it takes longer. Both fall.

items.p: Gurpreet and Lakshmi watched the balloon in the Let-Go Test. A grown-up reads what each one said. Say your answer out loud, and the grown-up writes it.

views.says: The balloon floated. It is so light that it doesn't really fall.
The balloon fell. It just fell slowly, and then it landed on the floor.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Say one thing the other child noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason from the test. Lakshmi is right that it landed. Gurpreet is right that it moved very slowly, as if floating, and that it is light.
items.why: The balloon did fall, all the way to the floor. But Gurpreet saw something true: it moved so slowly that it seemed to float, because the air slowed it.

items.p: Three of these fall when you let go. One goes up. Which one goes up?
opts: A helium balloon from a fair
items.why: A helium balloon goes up, because the heavier air around it pushes it up. The others fall down.

items.p: Draw yourself jumping. Then draw yourself landing. Draw an arrow to show the Earth's pull.
items.a: Two pictures: the child in the air, then on the ground, with an arrow pointing down.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the child comes back down, and the arrow points down towards the ground.

items.p: A girl called Kiran squashes a sheet of paper into a tight ball. She drops it next to a flat sheet of the same paper. Which one lands first?
items.why: The ball lands first. It is the same paper, but the flat sheet is wide, so the air slows it down more.

items.p: Draw the dot on the newspaper. Draw the lemon falling onto it. Then draw the path a sheet of paper took as it fell.
items.a: A straight line down onto the dot for the lemon, and a wobbly, swinging line for the paper, landing away from the dot.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lemon going straight down and the paper swinging from side to side, because the air pushes the paper about.

items.p: Put these in order. A grown-up reads them.
items: Anjali holds the ball up high.
a: Anjali holds the ball up high.
items.why: The ball falls only after Anjali's hand stops holding it.

items.p: A cup standing still on a table is not being pulled by the Earth.
items.why: False. The Earth pulls the cup all the time. The table holds it up. In Take Away the Holder, the tumbler fell the moment the book went, so the pull was there all along.

items.p: Ishita and her brother Farhan are watching a kite bird circling high over Kolkata. A grown-up reads what each one said. Say your answer out loud, and the grown-up writes it.

views.says: She is not falling because she is so light.
She is not falling because her wings push on the air, and the air holds her up.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For Ishita: when the bird folds her wings, she swoops down, so the wings are holding her up. For Farhan: birds are light for their size, and that helps.
items.why: Both see something true. Birds have light bodies for their size, which helps them fly. But a light bird still falls when she folds her wings. Her spread wings push the air down, and the air pushes her up.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to the way it falls.
pairs: Swinging from side to side, slowly
Down, bounces up a little, then down again
items.why: Everything falls, but in different ways. The air swings a leaf about, and a ball bounces before it stops.
items.art: A stone, a leaf, a rubber ball and a tap on the left, and four small drawings of falling paths on the right.

items.p: Look at the picture of a kitchen. A grown-up points to each thing. Say what is holding it up, and the grown-up writes it.
items.why: Every thing that is not falling has a support. A strong answer names a real support for each one.
items.art: A kitchen with a pressure cooker on a gas stove, steel tumblers on a shelf, a clock on a nail and a tawa hanging on a hook, each with an empty label.

items.p: In the Wall Marble Run, a girl called Kavya puts the marble at the top. Which way does the marble always end up going?
opts: Up to the top of the door
It stays where she put it
items.why: The Earth pulls the marble down. The tubes only change the path it takes.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it: a friend says rain falls because the clouds throw it down. What really makes raindrops come down?
items.a: The Earth's pull, gravity, brings the raindrops down.
items.why: A strong answer says the Earth pulls the raindrops down, the same way it pulls a spoon.

items.p: If someone took the floor away, you would stay up in the air.
items.why: False. The floor is what holds you up. Without it, the Earth's pull would make you fall, like the tumbler when the book went.

experiments.title: The Let-Go Test: does everything fall?
experiments.context: In this experiment you collect ten things from around the home. First you guess which ones will fall and which will stay up. Then you let go of each one and watch.
experiments.question: When you let go of something, does it always fall? Are there things that stay up in the air?
experiments.predict: Put each thing on the FALLS sheet or the STAYS UP sheet. Which ones will fall? Will any stay up? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We let go of every thing in the same way, from the same height, just by opening our hand. We do not throw or push, because a throw is a push. We only want to see what happens when nothing holds the thing.
results_table: My guess: falls or stays up?
What happened: fell fast, fell slowly, or stayed up?

materials.item: a steel spoon
a plastic bottle cap
a lemon, a small orange or a small ball
a sheet of paper
a ball of cotton wool
a feather, or a flower petal or a dry leaf if you have no feather
a balloon, blown up and tied by a grown-up
a pinch of rice
a spoonful of water
a dupatta or a hanky
a steel plate or thali to drop things onto
two sheets of paper: draw a big arrow pointing down and write FALLS on one, and draw a flat line and write STAYS UP on the other

schedule.what: Sort the ten things by your guesses, let go of each one, and move each to the sheet where it really belongs.

experiments.record: Draw the ten things on a page. Next to each, draw an arrow down if it fell. Colour the arrow red for fast and blue for slow. A grown-up can write the names.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: what happened to the ten things

setup.art: Ten everyday things laid out on a mat: a steel spoon, a bottle cap, a lemon, a sheet of paper, cotton wool, a feather, a balloon, rice, a spoon of water and a hanky.
setup.caption: 1. Collect ten things.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper on the floor, one with a big down arrow and one with a flat line, and a child placing the balloon on the flat-line sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Guess: put each thing on FALLS or STAYS UP.

setup.art: A girl standing over a steel plate, holding a spoon at shoulder height with an open hand just letting go.
setup.caption: 3. Hold it up. Open your hand. Watch.

setup.art: The same girl watching a balloon drift slowly down and land beside the plate.
setup.caption: 4. Watch to the very end. Where did it go?

flow.do: 1. Put the ten things on a mat. 2. Draw a big down arrow and write FALLS on one sheet. Draw a flat line and write STAYS UP on the other. Lay both sheets next to the things. 3. Name each thing together.
flow.say: Here are ten things from our home. When we let go of them, what will they do? Let's guess first.
flow.kid: Look at the ten things. Say the name of each one.
flow.parent: Blow up the balloon yourself and tie it. Leave a gap around you, away from the fan.

flow.do: Your child puts each thing on one of the two sheets, as a guess. Ask why for two or three of them.
flow.say: Put each thing on FALLS or STAYS UP. Which will fall? Will any stay up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put each thing on a sheet. Will it fall or stay up? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the balloon will stay up?
good: Because it is light and full of air.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Many children put the balloon, the feather and the cotton on STAYS UP. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands over the steel plate. 2. They hold each solid thing at shoulder height and open their hand. 3. Do the spoon, the cap, the lemon, the rice and the water.
flow.say: Hold the spoon up. Don't throw it. Just open your hand. Where did it go? Now the rice. Listen to it land.
flow.kid: Hold the spoon up. Open your hand. Where did it go?

ask.q: Which way did the spoon go?

flow.parent: For the water, hold the spoon over the plate and tip it. The water falls in drops or a little stream. Wipe up any spills so nobody slips.

flow.do: Now the light things: the paper, the cotton, the feather, the hanky and the balloon. Let go of each one at shoulder height. Watch each one until it lands.
flow.say: Now the light things. Watch the balloon very carefully. Don't look away until it stops moving. Did it stay up?
flow.kid: Let go of the feather. Watch it all the way. Did it land?

ask.q: What did the balloon do?
good: It floated down and landed on the floor.

flow.parent: Light things may drift sideways or float for a few seconds. Keep watching together until each one lands. If the fan is on, switch it off and try again.

flow.do: Move each thing to the sheet it really belongs on. Count what is left on STAYS UP.
flow.say: Let's move everything to where it really went. How many things are left on STAYS UP?
flow.kid: Move each thing to the right sheet. Is anything left on STAYS UP?

ask.q: How many things stayed up?

flow.parent: The STAYS UP sheet ends up empty. That surprise is the heart of the test.

flow.do: Ask what your child found, and why they think it happened. Then the check question.
flow.say: What did you find out? Why do you think everything fell, even the balloon?
flow.kid: What did you find out? Why did everything fall?

ask.q: What did you find out?
good: Some things fell fast and some fell slowly.

check.q: A girl called Kavya lets go of a feather. What will the feather do?
check.why: In the Let-Go Test, the feather fell slowly and landed. The air slows a feather down, but it still falls.

flow.parent: Wait for your child's own words first. Then say it plainly: everything falls when we let go. The Earth pulls everything down. Scientists call this pull gravity.

experiments.title: Right on the Dot: where does it land?
experiments.context: In this experiment you draw a dot on a newspaper and try to drop a lemon onto it. Then you try a sheet of paper, and see where that lands.
experiments.question: When you let go of something, where does it land? Right under your hand, or somewhere else?
experiments.predict: If you hold a lemon right above the dot and let go, will it land on the dot? Will a sheet of paper land on the dot too? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We hold each thing right above the dot, at the same height, and just open our hand. We try each one three times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: My guess: on the dot or away?

materials.item: a big sheet of newspaper
a marker, a crayon or a piece of chalk to draw a big dot
a lemon or a small ball
a bottle cap
a sheet of paper, the size of a notebook page
a few small coins or buttons, to mark where things land

schedule.what: Guess, drop the lemon, the cap and the paper onto the dot three times each, and mark where they land.

experiments.record: Draw the dot. Draw a small cross for each place the lemon landed, and a different colour cross for the paper.

setup.art: A big round dot drawn in the middle of a sheet of newspaper on a tiled floor.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a big dot on the newspaper.

setup.art: A girl bending a little, holding a lemon at chest height, looking down to line it up above the dot.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the lemon right above the dot.

setup.art: The lemon sitting on the dot, and a sheet of paper rocking down sideways and landing far from the dot.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. Then try a sheet of paper.

flow.do: 1. Spread the newspaper on the floor. 2. Your child draws a big dot in the middle, as wide as a steel katori.
flow.say: Let's draw a target. Make a big dot in the middle of the paper.
flow.kid: Draw a big dot in the middle of the newspaper.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before any drops.
flow.say: If you hold the lemon right above the dot and let go, where will it land? And the paper? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where will the lemon land? And the paper? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the lemon at chest height, right above the dot. 2. They look down to line it up. 3. They open their hand. 4. Put a coin where it first touched. Do it three times, then three times with the cap.
flow.say: Look down. Is the lemon right above the dot? Now open your hand. Where did it land? Let's do it again.
flow.kid: Hold the lemon over the dot. Look down. Let go. Where did it land?

ask.q: Where did the lemon land?

flow.parent: The lemon may roll after it lands. Mark the spot where it first touched the paper, not where it rolled to.

flow.do: Now your child holds the sheet of paper flat at chest height, right above the dot, and lets go. Do it three times. Mark where it lands each time.
flow.say: Now the paper. Hold it flat above the dot. Let go. Did it land on the dot? What did it do on the way down?
flow.kid: Hold the paper flat over the dot. Let go. Where did it go?

ask.q: What did the paper do?
good: It rocked from side to side.
It slid away and landed off the dot.

flow.parent: A flat sheet usually swings and slides sideways, so it often lands away from the dot. The air pushes it about. It still always comes down.

flow.do: Ask what your child found. Then the check question.
flow.say: Where did the lemon land each time? Where did the paper land? Why do you think they were different?
flow.kid: Where did the lemon land? Where did the paper land? Why?

check.q: A girl called Diya holds a ball right above a steel bowl and lets go. Where will the ball land?
options: In the bowl, right under her hand
It will stay in the air
check.why: A ball falls straight down, to the spot under where you let go. So it lands in the bowl.

flow.parent: Say it plainly after your child has spoken: a lemon falls straight down, to the spot right under your hand. A flat paper is pushed about by the air, but it still falls.

activities.title: Take Away the Holder
activities.context: In this activity a steel tumbler sits on a book, and a key hangs on a thread. You find out what is holding each one up, and what happens when the holder goes. Then you hunt for holders all around your home.

materials.item: a steel tumbler or a plastic cup, nothing that can break
a hardback book or a steel plate
a cushion or a pillow, to land on
a key or a hair clip, tied to a piece of thread about as long as your arm

schedule.what: Pull the book from under the tumbler, let go of the thread, then hunt for holders around the home.

activities.record: Draw one thing in your home and the holder that holds it up. Draw an arrow down to show the Earth's pull.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a book flat above a cushion, with a steel tumbler standing on the book.
setup.caption: 1. The tumbler sits on the book.

setup.art: The grown-up sliding the book away sideways, and the tumbler falling onto the cushion.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the book away. What happens?

setup.art: A child pointing up at a ceiling fan, and a clock on the wall, in a living room.
setup.caption: 3. Hunt for holders: what holds up the fan and the clock?

flow.do: 1. Hold the book flat above the cushion, at your child's chest height. 2. Stand the tumbler on the book. 3. Ask the question. 4. Slide the book away sideways, quickly.
flow.say: The tumbler is not falling. What is holding it up? What will happen if I take the book away? Watch.
flow.kid: The tumbler is not falling. What holds it up? Watch the book go.

ask.q: What held the tumbler up?
What happened when the book went?
good: It fell straight down onto the cushion.

flow.do: Your child holds the end of the thread so the key hangs down. Then they let go of the thread, over the cushion.
flow.say: What is holding the key up now? What will happen if you let go of the thread? Try it.
flow.kid: Hold the thread. What holds the key up? Now let go.

ask.q: What held the key up?

flow.do: Walk around the home together. Point to five things that are up off the floor. For each one, your child says what holds it up.
flow.say: Look at the fan. Why isn't it falling? What is holding it up? Now the clock. Now find something else that is up off the floor. What about you?
flow.kid: Look at the fan. What holds it up? Now find four more things.

ask.q: What holds you up right now?

flow.parent: Good holders to find: the ceiling hook for the fan, a nail for a clock or a photo, a shelf, pegs on a washing line, the stove under a cooker. The floor holds up everything in the end.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One question about holders.
flow.kid: Answer one question.

check.q: A girl called Lakshmi hangs a towel on a hook. What happens if the hook breaks?
options: The towel stays in the air
check.why: The hook was the towel's support. Without a support, the Earth's pull makes the towel fall.

activities.title: Falling Watch: the tap and the window
activities.context: In this activity you watch water fall from a tap, then look out of a window for five minutes and count everything that falls.

materials.item: a kitchen or bathroom tap and a bucket or a mug
a window or a balcony
paper and a pencil for tally marks

schedule.what: Watch the tap, then watch out of a window and count falling things.

activities.record: Draw the tap with water falling. Then draw the falling things you saw from the window, with a tally mark for each.

setup.art: A child watching a thin stream of water fall from a kitchen tap into a steel mug.
setup.caption: 1. Turn the tap on a little. Watch the water.

setup.art: A girl at a flat window making tally marks on paper, with leaves and raindrops falling outside.
setup.caption: 2. Watch from the window. Make a mark for each falling thing.

flow.do: Turn a tap on just a little, so a thin stream comes out. Your child watches where the water goes. Then pour water from one mug into another.
flow.say: Watch the water from the tap. Which way does it go? Could you ever make it fall up?
flow.kid: Watch the water. Which way does it go?

ask.q: Which way did the water go?

flow.parent: In most flats the water comes from a tank on the roof, down the pipes to your tap. The Earth's pull brings it to you.

flow.do: Sit at a window or on the balcony for five minutes. Your child makes a tally mark for every falling thing they see.
flow.say: Let's watch for five minutes. Every time you see something fall, make a mark. Leaves, rain, a dropped peg, water from a pipe.
flow.kid: Watch the window. Every time something falls, make a mark.

ask.q: What did you see falling?
good: Water dripping from the air conditioner pipe.

flow.parent: On a dry day, there may be only a few things. Look for leaves, drips from a pipe or an air cooler, and a peg or a petal that has come off. If there is nothing at all, drop a leaf from a potted plant yourself.

flow.do: Count the marks together. Then the check question.
flow.say: How many falling things did you see? Did anything fall up?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Did anything fall up?

check.q: A girl called Bornali has a potted plant. A dry leaf comes off. Where does the leaf go?
check.why: The Earth pulls the leaf down. The leaf sways because the air pushes it about, but it always lands.

activities.title: Fall Like a Leaf, Fall Like a Stone
activities.context: In this activity your body becomes a falling thing. The grown-up names a thing, and you fall down onto a mat the way that thing falls. Then you jump, and see if you can stay up.

materials.item: a mat, a mattress or a soft rug
a little space to move, away from furniture

schedule.what: Fall like a stone, a leaf, a feather, a raindrop and a balloon, then try to jump and stay up.

activities.record: Draw yourself falling like your favourite thing.

setup.art: A child crouching down quickly onto a mat like a stone, next to a picture of a stone.
setup.caption: 1. Fall like a stone: fast and straight.

setup.art: A child swaying slowly from side to side as she sinks down to the mat like a leaf.
setup.caption: 2. Fall like a leaf: slow and swaying.

setup.art: A child in the middle of a jump, both feet off the mat, arms up.
setup.caption: 3. Jump! Can you stay up?

flow.do: Name one thing at a time: a stone, a leaf, a feather, a raindrop, a balloon, a ball. Your child falls gently down onto the mat the way it falls.
flow.say: You are a stone. Let go! Now you are a leaf. How does a leaf fall? Now a feather. Now a ball. What does a ball do when it lands?
flow.kid: Be a stone. Fall down fast. Now be a leaf. Fall down slowly.
flow.parent: Your child should go down by bending their knees and sitting or lying on the mat, not by toppling over. A ball can bounce up once or twice before it stops.

flow.do: Your child jumps as high as they can, three times, and tries to stay up.
flow.say: Now jump as high as you can. Try to stay up in the air. Did you stay up? What brought you down?
flow.kid: Jump high. Try to stay up. What brought you down?

ask.q: What brought you down?

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One question about jumping.
flow.kid: Answer one question.

check.q: A girl called Zoya jumps as high as she can. What happens next?
options: She stays up in the air
check.why: The Earth pulls Zoya down, so every jump ends back on the ground.

projects.title: The Wall Marble Run
projects.context: In this project you tape paper tubes onto a cupboard door or a wall, sloping down, so a marble rolls from tube to tube all the way to a bowl at the bottom.

materials.item: 4 to 6 empty tubes from toilet rolls or kitchen rolls, or newspaper rolled into tubes
masking tape or sticky tape
a marble, a small ball or a round bead
a cupboard door, a fridge door or a wall where tape is allowed
a bowl or a box to catch the marble at the bottom
scissors, for a grown-up

projects.safety: Marbles and beads can choke babies and toddlers. Keep them out of reach of little brothers and sisters.

schedule.what: Cut some tubes in half to make open chutes, and tape the first tubes onto the door, sloping down.
Add more tubes, test the marble run, and try to make the marble go uphill.

projects.record: Draw your marble run. Draw arrows showing which way the marble went at each tube.

setup.art: Paper tubes, some cut in half lengthwise to make open chutes, a roll of masking tape and a marble on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Get your tubes and tape.

setup.art: A child taping a tube onto a cupboard door at a slant, with a grown-up holding it in place.
setup.caption: 2. Tape the tubes on, each one sloping down.

setup.art: A finished zig-zag marble run of paper tubes on a cupboard door, with a marble dropping into a steel bowl at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Drop the marble in at the top. Where does it end up?

flow.do: A grown-up cuts two or three tubes in half the long way, to make open chutes. Keep the other tubes whole.
flow.say: We will make a path for a marble, down a cupboard door. Some tubes we keep whole. Some we cut open, so we can watch the marble roll.
flow.kid: We are making a path for a marble. It goes down the door.
flow.parent: Cut away from your hands. Your child can hold the tube steady.

flow.do: Tape the first tube high up on the door, sloping down. Tape the next one below it, sloping the other way, so the marble drops from one into the next.
flow.say: Which way should the tube slope so the marble rolls? Let's tape it on. Now the next one goes under the end of this one.
flow.kid: Tape a tube on the door. Make it slope down. Add one more underneath.

ask.q: Why does the tube need to slope down?
good: So the marble can roll down.
The Earth pulls the marble down the slope.

flow.wait: Leave the run on the door until tomorrow.

flow.do: Add more tubes until the run reaches the bowl. Your child drops the marble in at the top. Fix any tube where the marble falls out.
flow.say: Drop the marble in at the top. Watch it go. Where did it fall out? How can we fix that tube?
flow.kid: Drop the marble in. Watch it go. Did it reach the bowl?
flow.parent: If the marble falls out, the next tube is too far away or not under the end. Move it closer.

flow.do: Tape one tube at the end sloping upwards. Your child tries to make the marble climb it.
flow.say: Can you make the marble roll uphill? Try it. How far up does it go?
flow.kid: Can the marble roll uphill? Try it. What happens?

ask.q: What happened on the uphill tube?
good: It went up a little, then came back.
It could not climb to the top.

flow.parent: A fast marble can roll a little way uphill, then it rolls back. It never climbs higher than where it started. The Earth's pull wins in the end.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One question about the marble run.
flow.kid: Answer one question.

check.q: A girl called Revathi makes a marble run and puts a marble at the top. Which way does it always go in the end?
options: Down to the bowl at the bottom
check.why: The Earth pulls the marble down. The tubes only change the path it takes on the way down.

challenges.title: Hold Up a Toy Without Your Hands
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must make a small toy stay up in the air, off the floor and off any table, for one whole minute, without holding it.
challenges.problem: Malini wants her small teddy to stay up in the air for one minute, so she can draw a picture of it. She cannot hold it, and it cannot sit on the floor, a table, a bed or a shelf. How can she keep it up?
constraints: The toy must be up in the air, not sitting on a floor, table, bed or shelf.
The toy must stay up for one whole minute.
materials: a dupatta or a long scarf
a door with a handle, or a chair
general: A cradle hangs from a hook or a beam, and holds a baby up.
Clothes pegs hold wet clothes up on a washing line.
Cable cars, like the ones in Gangtok and other hill towns, hang from strong cables.
creative: Tie a dupatta to a door handle and make a little hammock for the toy.
Peg the toy's ear to a clothes hanger and hang the hanger on a hook.
Put the toy in a cloth bag and hang the bag from the back of a chair.
challenges.your_turn: Find two different ways to keep the toy up. What is the toy's support each time? What happens if you take that support away?

setup.art: A small teddy on a mat, and next to it a dupatta, string, clothes pegs, a hanger and a cloth bag.
setup.caption: 1. The toy must stay up. What could hold the toy?

setup.art: A small soft toy in a little dupatta hammock tied to a door handle, and a girl watching a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. Make a holder. Can the toy stay up for one minute?

flow.do: Read the problem. Put the toy and the materials on the floor.
flow.say: The toy has to stay up in the air for one minute. You can't hold the toy. What could hold the toy up instead?
flow.kid: The toy must stay up. You can't hold the toy. What could hold the toy?

ask.q: What could hold the toy up?

flow.do: Your child tries their ideas. Time one minute for each. Help with knots only if asked.
flow.say: Try your idea. Start the timer. Is the toy still up? What is holding the toy now?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Is the toy still up? What is holding the toy?
flow.parent: If the toy keeps slipping, ask where the toy is slipping from, and what could hold that part.

flow.do: Ask what worked, and what the support was. Then the check question.
flow.say: Which way worked best? What was the toy's support? What would happen if we cut the string?
flow.kid: What held the toy up? What if we cut the string?

check.q: Malini's teddy hangs from a string. She cuts the string. What happens?
options: The teddy stays up in the air
check.why: The string was the teddy's support. Without it, the Earth's pull makes the teddy fall.

videos.title: A water drop falling and splashing, filmed in slow motion
videos.why: Shows a single drop falling straight down and landing, slowly enough to watch.
videos.check: Find a real slow-motion clip of a falling water drop from a science channel. Check that it is real footage, not animation.

videos.title: A kite or an eagle soaring and swooping
videos.why: Shows a bird staying up on spread wings and swooping down when she folds them, like the kite in the story.
videos.check: Find a real nature clip of a black kite or a similar bird soaring and diving. Check that it shows wings spread and then tucked in.

videos.title: Jog Falls in Karnataka during the monsoon
videos.why: Shows a huge amount of water falling straight down a cliff, pulled by the Earth.
videos.check: Find a real clip of Jog Falls in the monsoon, from a news channel or a travel channel. Check that it is the real place.

quiz.p: A baby opens his hand and lets go of a steel spoon. What does the spoon do?
quiz.why: Nothing holds the spoon now, so it falls down.

quiz.p: Which of these falls slowly when you let go?
quiz.why: The air slows down light, wide things like cotton wool. They still fall, only slowly.

quiz.p: What do scientists call the pull of the Earth that makes things fall?
quiz.why: The Earth's pull is called gravity.

quiz.p: What pulls a ripe mango down from the tree?
quiz.why: Gravity, the pull of the Earth, brings the mango down. Wind can shake a mango loose, but gravity makes it fall.

quiz.p: A girl called Sana has a photo frame on a nail. What is holding the frame up?
quiz.why: The nail is the frame's support. Without it, the frame would fall.

quiz.p: What is holding you up when you stand in your room?
quiz.why: The floor is your support. The Earth pulls you down, and the floor holds you up.

quiz.p: A girl called Malini puts a mug right under a dripping tap. Where do the drops land?
opts: In the mug, straight below the tap
On the wall behind the mug
They go up into the tap
quiz.why: A drop falls straight down, to the spot right under where it left the tap.

quiz.p: Which way is 'down', anywhere on the Earth?
quiz.why: Down always means towards the ground, because the Earth pulls everything towards it.

quiz.p: A girl called Jyoti is looking out of the window in Kochi during the monsoon. Which of these does she see falling?
opts: The clouds coming down to the street
quiz.why: Raindrops fall from the clouds to the ground, pulled by the Earth.

quiz.p: Why does a feather fall more slowly than a steel spoon?
opts: The air slows the feather down
The Earth does not pull the feather
quiz.why: The Earth pulls both. The feather is light and wide, so the air gets in its way.

applications: Water tanks sit on the roofs of buildings, so the water falls down the pipes to every tap in every flat.
Water falling from high dams, such as the Idukki dam in Kerala, turns machines that make electricity.
Playground slides work because the Earth pulls you down the slope.
Builders hang a heavy weight on a string, called a plumb line, to find straight down, so their walls stand straight.
Mango pickers use a long pole with a little bag at the top, so the falling mangoes drop into the bag, not onto the ground.

spotted.text: Monsoon rain in Kochi falling from the sky and running down the window glass.
spotted.art: Heavy rain falling past a window, with drops running down the glass and coconut palms outside.

spotted.text: Jog Falls in Karnataka, where a river falls down a tall cliff.
spotted.art: A tall waterfall pouring down a rocky cliff into a misty gorge, with green forest around it.

spotted.text: Shiuli flowers in West Bengal, which fall from the tree in the early morning and cover the ground.
spotted.art: A carpet of small white flowers with orange stems on the ground under a tree, at dawn.

spotted.text: Dahi Handi in Mumbai, where a pot of curd hangs on a rope high above the street until someone breaks it.
spotted.art: A clay pot hanging on a rope high above a street, with a human pyramid reaching up towards it.

spotted.text: A coconut falling from a tall palm in Goa or Kerala.
spotted.art: A brown coconut falling from the top of a tall palm tree towards the sand.

open_questions.q: How does the Earth pull a spoon without touching it?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure the pull very well, and have two good ideas about it. But nobody yet knows what gravity is at the very tiniest scale.

open_questions.q: Why is the Earth's pull so weak compared with a magnet's?
open_questions.why_open: A small fridge magnet can hold a steel pin up against the pull of the whole Earth. Scientists do not yet know why gravity is so much weaker than the other forces.

open_questions.q: Is gravity made of tiny pieces?
open_questions.why_open: Light comes in tiny pieces. Some scientists think gravity does too, but nobody has ever found one.

ask_kids: What is holding up the fan right now?
Can you find something in the kitchen that falls slowly?
If you let go of your idli, which way will it go?
Why do you think birds do not fall?
What is holding up our building?
Have you ever seen anything fall up?

jokes.j: Why did the lemon fall off the table?
jokes.a: It was feeling a bit down!

jokes.j: What did the floor say to the falling spoon?
Why was the feather always late?
jokes.a: It took the slow way down!

jokes.j: Why did the raindrop never get lost?
jokes.a: It always knew which way was down!

jokes.j: What did the balloon say to the spoon?
jokes.a: You go first. I'll be down in a minute!

jokes.j: Why did the mango leave the tree?
jokes.a: It was fed up with hanging around!

jokes.j: What did the teddy say when the string was cut?
Why did the clothes peg love the washing line?
jokes.a: Because they always hang out together!

maths.problem: A girl called Kavya did the Let-Go Test with a different ten things from yours. She counted 6 things that fell fast and 4 things that fell slowly. Did more things fall fast or slowly? How many things fell in all?
maths.answer: More fell fast. 10 things fell in all.
maths.explain: 6 is more than 4, so more fell fast. 6 and 4 make 10. That was every thing she tried, so nothing stayed up.
maths.context: This is about the Let-Go Test, where you let go of ten things.
maths.why_maths: Sorting and counting the results shows at a glance that every thing fell.

maths.problem: In Catch It Before It Lands, a girl called Lakshmi caught the hanky 3 times out of 3. She caught the sock ball only 1 time out of 3. Which one was easier to catch? Why do you think so?
maths.answer: The hanky was easier. It falls slowly, so she had more time.
maths.explain: 3 catches is more than 1 catch, so the hanky was easier. The hanky falls slowly because the air slows it down. The sock ball falls fast, so there is less time to catch it.
maths.context: This is about Catch It Before It Lands, where a grown-up dropped things for you to catch.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers tells us which thing was easier, and then we can think about why.

maths.problem: You hold a steel spoon over a plate and let go. Is it certain, possible or impossible that the spoon falls? Is it certain, possible or impossible that it floats up to the ceiling?
maths.answer: It is certain that it falls. It is impossible that it floats up.
maths.explain: In the Let-Go Test, everything we let go of fell. Nothing holds the spoon, and the Earth always pulls it. So falling is certain, and floating up is impossible.
maths.context: This is about the Let-Go Test, where every thing you let go of fell.
maths.why_maths: Words like certain and impossible help us say how sure we are, using what we found in the test.

links.title: NASA Space Place: What is gravity?
links.why: For the parent: a short, clear page from NASA about gravity, with pictures to look at together.

links.title: StoryWeaver, free picture books from Pratham Books
links.why: For the parent: free picture books in many Indian languages to read aloud. Search for books about rain, falling and flying.

links.title: Kerala State Science and Technology Museum
links.why: A science museum and planetarium with hands-on science galleries, good for a family day out.

warmup.q: Which way does a spoon go when you let go of it?
What is the Earth's pull called?
What holds up a ceiling fan?
What holds you up when you sit?
When you jump, what brings you back down?

roots.context: We have dropped spoons, rice, feathers and a balloon, and pulled a book from under a tumbler. Now we ask what all that falling tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Everything you let go of in the Let-Go Test fell, even the feather and the balloon. A thing stays up only while something holds it, like a hand, a shelf or the floor. Pull the book away, and the tumbler falls at once. So the Earth is pulling the tumbler all the time, even while it sits still.
deep_truth.habit: We think a thing sitting still has nothing happening to it, and that only falling things are being pulled. The tumbler on the book shows the pull was there all along. The book was holding it back.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Let-Go Test, all ten things fell when the child opened their hand, some fast and some slowly. In Take Away the Holder, the tumbler and the key stayed up while the book and the thread held them, and fell the moment those were taken away.

three.who_am_i: The Earth is pulling you right now, as you read or listen. The floor or your chair is holding you up.
three.what_is_life: Every living being lives with the Earth's pull. A plant's roots grow down and their stem grows up. A bird's spread wings hold her up on the air.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth pulls everything near it: spoons, rain, air and even the Moon. Nothing near the Earth is left out.

roots.thread: Everything near the Earth is pulled towards it, all the time. We notice the pull only when something falls. A tumbler on a table, a fan on the ceiling and a child on the floor are being pulled too, and held. Holding and pulling go on together, every second, all around us.

teachings.source: Atharva Veda 12.1, the hymn to the Earth (verse 6)
teachings.teaching: The hymn calls the Earth the bearer of all, the holder of treasures, and the firm ground on which every moving thing rests.
teachings.link: In Take Away the Holder, every falling thing ended up on the floor, and the floor rests on the ground. The hymn praises the Earth for holding everything up. Science adds that the Earth also pulls everything down onto itself.

teachings.teaching: The highest good is like water. Water helps all things and does not fight. It flows to the low places that people look down on.
teachings.link: At the tap, the water always went down, to the lowest place it could reach. The Earth's pull is why water always finds the low places. The Tao Te Ching praises water for going there.

science.text: The Earth pulls everything near it towards its middle. This pull is called gravity.
Everything pulls on everything else, a tiny bit. You pull on the Earth too, but the Earth is far bigger, so you are the one who falls.
Nobody yet knows what gravity is at the very tiniest scale.

other_view.who: Albert Einstein, and many physicists today
other_view.view: Gravity is not really a pull. The Earth bends space and time around it, and a falling spoon simply follows that bend. Both ways of describing it give the same falls we see in the kitchen.

practice.title: Let the floor hold you
practice.say: Lie down on your back on the floor or a mat. Let your arms and legs go heavy. Feel where the floor touches you: your head, your back, your heels. The Earth is pulling you down. The floor is holding you up. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out. Lift one arm a little. Let it drop softly onto the mat. What caught your arm?
practice.kid: Lie on your back. Let your arms go heavy. Feel the floor under you. The Earth pulls you. The floor holds you. Lift one arm. Let it flop down. What caught it?

ask: When you sit still on a chair, is the Earth still pulling you? How could you tell?
What holds up the floor of your home? And what holds that up?
Could anything stay up with nothing at all holding it?
roots.art: A child lying on her back on a mat with her arms spread and eyes closed, a ceiling fan above her.

how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, people thought some things fall and other things rise, just by their nature. About 2,350 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle taught this. Stones and water fall, he said, but smoke, air and fire go up. Many people agreed for about two thousand years. Then, in 1638, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei wrote about a test. He pushed extra air into a glass bottle and weighed it. Then he let the air out and weighed it again. The bottle was lighter, so air has weight, and the Earth pulls on air too. So why does smoke go up? Hot, smoky air is lighter than the cooler air around it. The heavier air sinks underneath and pushes the smoke up, the way water pushes a ball up in a bucket. Things go up only when something pushes them up.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker; Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought smoke, air and fire go up by nature, and are not pulled down. Galileo weighed air and found it has weight, so the Earth pulls air too. Smoke rises only because heavier air around it pushes it up.

founder: ideas/by_topic/gravity.md, Grade 1 concept: gravity keeps your feet on the floor, every jump comes back down, falling leaves and raindrops, and birds and balloons that seem to escape the pull but are using the air. These became the Let-Go Test, Fall Like a Leaf, the Falling Watch and the kite bird in the story.

ideas/by_topic/gravity.md: the note that the ground holds you up became Take Away the Holder and the toy challenge. The heavy-and-light drops, crumpled paper and the space-time blanket belong to the Level 3 unit, so this unit uses the let-go sort, the dot drop, the holder hunt and the marble run instead.
science: Aristotle, On the Heavens (De Caelo), Book 4: earth and water move down by nature, fire and air move up.
Galileo Galilei, Two New Sciences (1638), First Day: weighing a glass vessel with extra air forced into it, to show that air has weight.
Archimedes' principle: a thing in a liquid or a gas is pushed up by the weight of what it pushes aside, which is why helium balloons and hot smoke rise.
Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), the law of universal gravitation. Albert Einstein, general relativity (1915).
Gravitropism: plant roots grow down and shoots grow up in response to gravity.
Atharva Veda 12.1 (Prithvi Sukta), verse 6, and Tao Te Ching, chapter 8.
